description:
Scripture supplies the basis for distinguishing the renewed heart from the flesh. Returning to the previous diagram, Wesam Saad asks listeners to test its claims through the biblical passages rather than accept them on his authority. His reading of Romans 6 connects the crucifixion of the old self with a new inward life directed towards God. The continuing commands concern what believers do with their bodily members and desires. They are to recognise what has already happened in regeneration and act on it, presenting themselves and their bodies to God. Saad describes this as a real capacity for obedience that should lead to gratitude and purposeful resistance to sin.

Romans 7 then provides his account of the conflict: the inward person delights in God’s law while sinful desires remain in the flesh. Saad rejects the description of this as two competing natures and cautions against treating an editorial Bible heading as the text itself. Passages about desires, conflict and the redemption of the body extend the explanation. The heart is again compared to a receiving stomach that needs nourishment. The closing encouragement is that immaturity need not mean defeat: believers should feed the new life God has given, resist the passions opposing it and continue growing towards Christ.

questions.question: Why does this session return to the diagram through extended Scripture reading?
questions.answer: Saad wants listeners to assess the explanation from the biblical text rather than accept it merely because he has taught it. The recap establishes the terms, then the passages are used to distinguish the inward person, bodily members and remaining desires. The diagram serves the reading rather than replacing it.

questions.question: How does Saad connect the old self’s crucifixion with new life in Romans 6?
questions.answer: He identifies the old self with the former heart and reads its crucifixion as a decisive event. In his explanation, the new inward life is now alive to God, while the body still contains desires that must be brought under control. Regeneration is therefore distinguished from the continuing work of growth.

questions.question: What does he mean by recognising oneself as dead to sin?
questions.answer: Saad distinguishes recognising what God has already done from trying to make regeneration happen repeatedly. He says that the believer’s new life provides the basis for refusing the rule of sinful desires. Recognition should lead to obedience rather than passive satisfaction with a doctrinal statement.

questions.question: What choice is involved in presenting bodily members?
questions.answer: The teacher says believers can present their members as instruments of righteousness rather than serving sinful desires. He places responsibility for that choice on the believer and links it with sanctification. The new inward life is presented as the reason that resistance and obedient action are possible.

questions.question: Why does Saad question the heading about two natures above Romans 7?
questions.answer: He distinguishes an editorial heading from Scripture and argues that the passage describes a conflict between the renewed inward person and the flesh. He reads the inward delight in God’s law and the opposing desires in bodily members as different aspects of that conflict, not two enduring hearts or natures.

questions.question: Why does the discussion go beyond changing outward behaviour?
questions.answer: Saad draws attention to the desires and pleasures beneath actions, including the conflicts described by James. He contrasts mere behavioural adjustment with resisting sinful desires and cultivating godly ones. His concern is that obedience should involve the inward struggle rather than leave its motives untouched.

questions.question: What does the stomach analogy add to the description of the new heart?
questions.answer: The heart is pictured as receiving and digesting nourishment before producing fruit. Saad connects this with God’s word, beholding Christ and the enjoyment of God. The analogy explains why a new heart still needs to grow and why inward impressions do not become the believer’s final authority.

questions.question: What hope does the teacher give to an immature believer facing strong desires?
questions.answer: He argues that the new life God has given makes resistance possible even when old passions seem powerful. The response is to continue receiving nourishment and taking steps in obedience rather than give up. Growth is described as progressive, not as an instant absence of conflict.
